Individual Project, DSCI 100 (80 points)¶

INSTRUCTIONS¶

Complete the following questions individually using the provided data set. When prompted, fill out the cells with your code (in code cells) or text (in text cells) to answer the question. The cells will have "%%% EDIT THIS MARKDOWN CELL %%%" or "### EDIT THIS CODE CELL ###" prompting you to overwrite the contents of the cell with your answer.

Your report must be fully reproducible, and run without error by itself with no other files.

REFERENCES¶

Students are required to use methods discussed in DSCI 100 for the project report. However, there may be some stages where you wish to research on how to handle "messy" data, including outliers, missing data, etc. If you refer to anything beyond DSCI 100, please include a link to the reference at the end of this report. It does not need to be a "formal" reference like an academic paper or website, you can link to blog posts or websites like StackExchange if they are relevant to your analysis.

GENERATIVE AI USE¶

This analysis is based on methods learned in DSCI 100, so you should have all of the tools you need to write this code from scratch. You may use Generative AI (i.e., ChatGPT, Gemini, etc) as an "advanced search engine" (i.e., to help de-bug code).You cannot use it to generate code or text on the report. Any use of Generative AI must be disclosed at the bottom of this project report.

An example of a disclosure of appropriate Gen AI use: "I tried to fit a model using function X and got error Y. Gen AI helped me figure out that the error was due to a missing value."

Failure to disclose Generative AI use is a form of academic misconduct. Submissions suspected of inappropriately using Gen AI will be flagged by the teaching team and handled on a case-by-base basis.

Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Visualization 1: This boxplot compares regional win percentages between teams with automatic and at-large bids. It helps us examine whether regional win percentage differs between the two groups. If their distributions are different, regional win percentage may be useful for predicting bid type.

In [9]:
ggplot(tidy_data, aes(x = bid, y = reg_wins_pct, fill = bid)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Regional Win Percentage by Bid Type",
    x = "Bid Type",
    y = "Regional Win Percentage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

This scatterplot shows the relationship between regional wins and regional win percentage, with points colored by bid type. It helps us investigate whether the two predictors together can distinguish automatic bids from at-large bids. If the two groups form separate clusters, these variables may be useful for classification.

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I plan to use K-nearest neighbours (KNN) classification to predict a team's bid type using regional wins ("reg_wins") and regional win percentage ("reg_wins_pct"). This method is appropriate because the target variable ("bid") is categorical, and KNN predicts a category based on the most similar observations.

One limitation of KNN is that its performance depends on the choice of K. It is also sensitive to differences in the scales of predictors and may perform poorly when different categories overlap.

I will first remove observations with missing values in the relevant variables. Then, I will split the data into 80% training data and 20% testing data, using stratified sampling based on bid type. I will center and scale the predictors using the training data to prevent variables with larger scales from dominating the distance calculations.

I will use 5-fold cross-validation on the training set to select an appropriate K value. After selecting K, I will fit the final model using the training data and evaluate it on the testing data.

I will assess model performance using classification accuracy and a confusion matrix. Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions, while the confusion matrix shows which bid types are incorrectly classified.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(9999)

# Remove missing values and convert bid to a factor
model_data <- tidy_data |>
  drop_na(reg_wins_pct, reg_wins, bid) |>
  mutate(bid = as_factor(bid))

Task 5.3 Create a Visualization or Table of the Results of your Analysis (4 points)¶

  • Create a visualization or table that is relevant to the results of your analysis (comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow).
  • Describe what this visualization or table is showing, and why it is important to the analysis (approx 150 words or less).

The confusion matrix shows the performance of the K-nearest neighbors classification model by comparing the predicted bid types with the actual bid types. The model correctly classified 173 at-large bids and 95 automatic bids, achieving an overall accuracy of approximately 63.96%. However, 104 automatic bids were incorrectly classified as at-large bids. This visualization is important because it shows not only the overall performance of the model but also which category is more difficult to predict. The model performs better when predicting at-large bids than automatic bids.

  )

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

The purpose of this analysis was to investigate whether regional win percentage and regional wins could be used to predict whether a team received an automatic or at-large bid in the NCAA Women's Basketball Tournament. The K-nearest neighbors classification model achieved a testing accuracy of approximately 63.96%. Although the two predictors provided some useful information, the model was not highly accurate. The confusion matrix also showed that the model was better at identifying at-large bids than automatic bids. During the analysis, cross-validation was used to compare different values of K and select a suitable number of neighbors.

I expected teams' winning performance to be useful for predicting their bid types. However, the relatively low accuracy suggests that regional wins and regional win percentage alone may not be sufficient to distinguish between the two categories. Automatic bids also depend on conference qualification rules, which are not fully represented by these two predictors. In future analyses, additional variables, such as conference wins, conference win percentage, and conference rank, could be included to investigate whether they improve classification accuracy.
